Field surveys of Haemulon steindachneri along the Brazilian coast indicate that adults attain a maximum total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a size that positions this species among the medium-sized members of the genus. This ultimate length is typically reached by individuals in populations inhabiting rocky reef habitats with abundant shelter, where predation pressure from larger piscivores is moderate. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis suggest that most of the somatic expansion occurs during the first three years of life, after which the rate of length increase slows considerably as energy is increasingly allocated toward gonadal development. The body weight corresponding to this asymptotic length has been estimated at 403 grams [Wwi = 403 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a large sample of specimens collected across multiple seasons. This mass represents a substantial investment in somatic tissue that supports the species' relatively active foraging lifestyle on benthic invertebrates. Comparisons with sympatric congeners such as Haemulon plumierii show that H. steindachneri achieves a slightly smaller maximum size, which may reflect differences in diet composition and microhabitat use within the reef environment.

The onset of reproductive activity in this species is marked by the achievement of a total length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet weight of 49.4 grams [Wwp = 49.4 grams] based on the same length-weight relationship used for adults. Puberty at this moderate size suggests a life-history strategy that balances early maturation against continued somatic growth, a trade-off commonly observed in tropical reef fishes facing relatively high adult mortality. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals collected across the size gradient confirms that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis commence only after this size threshold is crossed. The ecological implication is that juveniles smaller than 15 centimeters remain in mixed-species foraging aggregations where they face reduced predation risk, whereas larger individuals begin to establish the solitary or pair-based territories associated with breeding. This pattern aligns with observations from other Haemulon species, where social structure shifts markedly at the transition to reproductive maturity. The relatively modest size at puberty also implies that the species can begin contributing to the next generation within a few years of settlement, a demographic characteristic that may buffer local populations against fishing pressure.

At a sustained water temperature of 27.1 °C [T = 27.1 °C], which is typical of the shallow coastal waters where this species is most abundant during the spawning season, individual females produce approximately 410 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 410 eggs per day] across the peak reproductive window. This daily output is sustained over a spawning period that extends for roughly 120 days per year, yielding an annual fecundity that is high relative to body size. The daily rate is a composite of multiple spawning events; field observations indicate that a single female releases between 1,000 and 2,000 eggs per distinct spawning bout [N_R_i = spawning events; field observations indicate that a single female releases between 1,000 and 2,000 eggs per distinct spawning bout], with such events occurring, on average, every 3 to 4 days [F_R_i = events occurring, on average, every 3 to 4 days] during the height of the reproductive season. This reproductive strategy, characterized by frequent, moderate-sized clutches, is typical of iteroparous tropical serranids and haemulids that inhabit stable thermal environments. The derivation of these estimates draws on comparative data from the congener Haemulon album, scaled according to adult body mass, which predicts an annual output of approximately 2.2 million eggs for a 403-gram female (403 grams) [Wwi = 403 grams]. The relatively high fecundity underscores the importance of larval survival in regulating population dynamics.

Newly hatched larvae of Haemulon steindachneri emerge from the chorion at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet weight of just 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams]. This minute body mass, typical of pelagic-spawning marine teleosts, corresponds to an egg diameter of approximately 0.85 millimeters, a value consistent with that reported for the closely related Lutjanus stellatus. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-eclosion, a period during which it remains in the upper water column and drifts with prevailing currents. The energetic constraints imposed by such a small starting mass are severe: the larva must begin exogenous feeding within a narrow window, typically no more than 3 to 4 days after hatching, before the yolk is fully resorbed. Field collections of ichthyoplankton along the southeastern Brazilian coast reveal that first-feeding larvae measure approximately 2.5 millimeters in standard length, underscoring the rapid growth required to transition successfully from lecithotrophic to exotrophic nutrition. The vulnerability of this early life stage to starvation and predation likely acts as a major bottleneck on recruitment, as has been demonstrated for many other reef-fish species with similar larval characteristics.

At 27.1 °C [T = 27.1 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for Haemulon steindachneri under natural conditions is 12 years [am = 12 years], based on mark-recapture data and validated otolith annulus counts from individuals collected in protected marine areas. This lifespan is attained at the same prevailing thermal regime that characterizes the species' core habitat, suggesting that metabolic rate and cellular senescence proceed at rates typical for a tropical teleost of this body size. Longevity estimates are comparable to those reported for other haemulids of similar ultimate length, though some congeneric species in cooler, higher-latitude waters may exceed 20 years. The trade-off between early maturity at 15 centimeters and a maximum lifespan of 12 years places this species toward the faster end of the life-history continuum within the family, a strategy that may be advantageous in environments where adult survival is less predictable. The presence of individuals approaching this age in no-take reserves indicates that protection from fishing can allow the species to realize its full physiological lifespan, which has positive implications for the reproductive contribution of older, larger females to the population's egg production.
